modules.title: What Is Philosophy
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 1 of Humanities for Technologists. I'm your instructor, and over the next fourteen modules we're going to build the disciplines of judgment that turn a capable builder into a senior technologist — someone whose decisions deserve trust. We start at the root: this module maps the branches of philosophy and shows how each one already lives in your technical work — logic in code, ethics in deployment, epistemology in science, aesthetics in design.
objectives: Name the major branches of philosophy and their questions
Connect each branch to a concrete technical practice
Distinguish philosophy from science and from opinion
Read a philosophical argument charitably before criticizing it

notes.body: **Deliverable: a one-page Branches Audit of a live project.** Pick a system you work on. For each of the six branches — logic, epistemology, metaphysics (what the system's data model claims exists), ethics, aesthetics, political philosophy (who holds power over the system) — write two sentences on where that branch's questions show up in the project. Close with one paragraph: which branch's questions is your team currently ignoring, and what is that neglect costing? This audit becomes your personal map for the rest of the course — revisit it in Module 14.

- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to sketch (in text) the anatomy of an argument — premises, inference, conclusion — using one of your own recent decisions as the example."

notes.title: Common mistakes: Logic & Argumentation

cards.back: Valid: conclusion must follow if premises true. Sound: valid + premises actually true.
Ponens: P→Q, P ⊢ Q. Tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P.
Deduction: certain, form-based. Induction: generalization from instances. Abduction: best-explanation inference.

cards.front: Define: straw man, false dilemma, post hoc.
cards.back: Straw man: attack a distortion. False dilemma: two options where more exist. Post hoc: after⇒because-of.

cards.front: Why is naming a fallacy not a complete rebuttal?
cards.back: You still owe the substantive counterargument — the label diagnoses, it doesn't refute by itself.

cards.front: Define: begging the question; appeal to authority.
cards.back: Begging the question (petitio principii): the conclusion is smuggled into a premise — the argument goes in a circle. Appeal to authority: accepting a claim because a prestigious source says so rather than because of evidence or reasoning. The module's CTO-Postgres example is an appeal to authority: the choice might be right, but the reason given is the wrong one. (Concepts.)

True is a property of propositions (they correspond to the facts). Valid is a property of arguments (the conclusion follows from the premises — the premises cannot be true while the conclusion is false). An argument can be valid with false premises, and a conclusion can be true while the argument for it is invalid. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Sketch a cogent inductive argument from operations.
cards.back: Inductive form: many observed instances → probably-general conclusion, strength graded by sample size, representativeness, and controls. Ops example: 'Of the last 40 deploys with this canary pattern, none caused an incident; so the next canary deploy is probably safe' — strong if the 40 are representative, weak if conditions changed. (Concepts.)
an argument whose conclusion is claimed to follow necessarily from its premises.
a deductive argument is valid if the conclusion *must* be true whenever the premises are; validity is about form, not content.
valid *and* with premises that are actually true.
if P then Q; P; therefore Q.

quiz.q: 'All servers are machines; db-1 is a server; therefore db-1 is a machine' is:
quiz.explain: Correct form (syllogism) with true premises — valid and sound. (See 'Concepts': valid, sound.)

quiz.q: 'Either we migrate now or the system collapses' — with no evidence of collapse — is:
quiz.explain: It asserts only two options without ruling out the rest — the false-dilemma pattern. (See 'Concepts': false dilemma.)

quiz.q: Inferring 'the cache is stale' as the best explanation of the symptoms is:
quiz.explain: Best-explanation inference from evidence — abduction, the logic of debugging. (See 'Concepts': abduction.)

quiz.q: 'The CTO prefers Postgres, so Postgres is the right choice' is:
quiz.explain: Status substitutes for reasons — the CTO's preference is not itself an argument. (See 'Concepts': appeal to authority.)

quiz.q: A sound argument requires premises that are:
choices: True, combined with a valid inference
quiz.explain: Sound = valid form + true premises. Persuasiveness is rhetoric, not logic. (Concepts.)

quiz.q: Affirming the consequent — 'if the cache is stale the page is slow; the page is slow; so the cache is stale' — is:
choices: A formal fallacy: the consequent does not determine the antecedent
quiz.explain: A slow page has many possible causes; the form 'if P then Q; Q; therefore P' is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. Denying the consequent would be valid (modus tollens). (Concepts.)

quiz.q: In the Hands-on procedure, the 'steel-man' step asks you to:
choices: Find the strongest version of the opposing argument
Name every fallacy in the opponent's case
quiz.explain: Steel-manning is charity in practice: rebuild the opponent's case at its strongest before rebutting, so the rebuttal actually lands. (Hands-on procedure.)

quiz.q: Abductive reasoning is best described as inference to:
choices: The best explanation of the evidence
quiz.explain: Abduction proposes the hypothesis that best explains the observations — the daily bread of debugging and incident response. (Concepts.)

modules.title: Ethics I — The Three Traditions
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3. I'm your instructor, and this is where judgment gets its frameworks: virtue ethics, deontology, and consequentialism — three traditions that answer 'what should I do?' with three different decision procedures. You'll apply all three to the same technical dilemma, and discover that their disagreements are the point.
objectives: State the core question of each tradition
Apply each to a technical dilemma
Compare how the three can disagree on one case
Recognize which tradition you default to

notes.title: Concepts
Hands-on procedure
Project brief
notes.body: **Deliverable: a two-page ethics review memo.** Take a real product decision — past or pending — and run all three traditions on it, following the Hands-on procedure. The memo must contain: the decision stated plainly, each tradition's analysis in its own section, the point of disagreement, and your recommendation with reasons. If all three traditions agree, say so and say why the case was easy; if they split, own the split.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- In one sentence, what question does each tradition ask? (Virtue: what kind of person should I be? Deontology: what is my duty? Consequentialism: which act has the best outcomes?)
- Give Noah the addictive-engagement feature and ask which tradition condemns it fastest — and on what grounds.
- *Visual learners:* "Ask Noah to lay out the three verdicts side by side for a deploy decision you are facing, then point to where they disagree."
- *Honesty:* these frameworks structure judgment; they do not automate it — a memo that cites a tradition without doing the analysis is ethics theater.

notes.title: Worked example: Ethics I — The Three Traditions
notes.body:
**Problem.** 'Would I endorse everyone doing this?' is the decision procedure of:
A. Virtue ethics
B. Deontology ←
C. Utilitarianism
D. Egoism

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Ethics I — The Three Traditions — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (Virtue ethics); C (Utilitarianism); D (Egoism) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: B. Universalizability is Kant's test — the first formulation of the categorical imperative. (See 'Concepts': Kant, categorical imperative.)

**Solution.** B — Deontology

*Try it yourself:* cover the solution, re-answer from memory, then check. If you missed it, re-read the Concepts note before moving on.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Ethics I — The Three Traditions

cards.front: Virtue ethics: core question and key figure?
cards.back: 'What kind of person should I be?' — Aristotle; virtues cultivated by habit.
Act only on universalizable maxims; treat humanity as an end, never merely as a means.

cards.front: Utilitarianism: core claim and key figures?
cards.back: Right act maximizes overall well-being — Bentham, Mill.
Virtue: vague guidance. Deontology: rigid, conflicting duties. Consequentialism: justifies sacrificing individuals; needs impossible predictions.

cards.front: State the decision procedure of each tradition in one line.
cards.back: Virtue: what would the good craftsperson do? Deontology: could I will this as universal law, and does it treat persons as ends? Utilitarianism: which act maximizes expected good outcomes?

cards.front: The three verdicts on an addictive-engagement feature — one line each?
cards.back: Virtue: does it express a good craftsperson's character? Deontology: does it treat users as mere means? Utilitarian: do aggregate harms outweigh engagement-happiness?

cards.front: State the trolley problem's function in ethics teaching.
cards.back: It isolates the clash between traditions: the utilitarian pulls the lever (minimize deaths); the Kantian objects (using the one as a mere means is forbidden regardless of outcome); the virtue ethicist asks what a person of practical wisdom would do. Its value is diagnostic, not decisive — it reveals which considerations your judgment actually weighs. (Concepts.)

cards.front: What is 'moral luck', and why does it matter for engineers?
cards.back: Moral luck: outcomes beyond our control (which deploy hits production at 3 AM, which bug ships on a Friday) affect blame and praise. **Problem.** A theory compatible with every possible observation is, for Popper:
A. The best kind of theory
B. Unscientific (unfalsifiable) ←
C. Probabilistically true
D. A paradigm

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Epistemology & Philosophy of Science — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (The best kind of theory); C (Probabilistically true); D (A paradigm) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: B. Falsifiability is the demarcation line: no forbidden observations, no science. (See 'Concepts': falsifiability.)

**Solution.** B — Unscientific (unfalsifiable)

*Try it yourself:* cover the solution, re-answer from memory, then check. If you missed it, re-read the Concepts note before moving on.

A. A heliocentric theory

cards.front: What made the Scientific Revolution methodologically new?
cards.back: Mathematized hypotheses tested against precise, often instrument-mediated measurement.

cards.front: Thales to Aristotle: the one-sentence story of Greek natural philosophy.
cards.back: Thales (~600 BCE) proposed a single natural principle (water) behind appearances — explanation without gods. The atomists (Democritus) added indivisible particles in void. cards.front: The Islamic Golden Age: three contributions the module names.
cards.back: Ibn al-Haytham's optics: controlled experiments with light, an early scientific method (~1000 CE). Al-Khwarizmi's algebra: systematic equation-solving — the root of 'algorithm'. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad: preservation and extension of Greek astronomy and medicine. (Concepts.)

cards.front: Why does the module call dates 'load-bearing'?
cards.back: Dates anchor causal order: you cannot claim Newton 'responded to' Einstein, or alchemy 'failed because of' chemistry before chemistry existed. Load-bearing dates prevent anachronism — the most common failure mode in technical histories of ideas. (Concepts.)

cards.back: The old theory survives as a limiting case — e.g., Newton inside Einstein at low speeds.

cards.front: The 1905 'miracle year': name the papers and their targets.
cards.back: Photoelectric effect (light quanta — the quantum seed), Brownian motion (atoms are real — the statistical proof), special relativity (space and time are not absolute), and E=mc² (mass–energy equivalence). One patent clerk, one year, four foundations. (Concepts.)

cards.front: The DNA double helix (1953): whose data, whose model?
cards.back: Franklin and Wilkins's X-ray diffraction (Photo 51) supplied the decisive structural data; Watson and Crick built the model that explained it. The module's lesson: credit follows the explanatory synthesis, but the synthesis needs the data — know both halves of the story. (Concepts.)

cards.front: How does the module say revolutions relate to old theories?
cards.back: New theories swallow the old as limiting cases: relativity reduces to Newton at low speeds, quantum mechanics to classical at large scales (the correspondence principle). Revolutions extend the domain of validity; they do not erase what worked. (Concepts.)
Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin: energy conservation and **entropy**; the science of engines became the science of everything.
*On the Origin of Species* (1859): **natural selection** explains adaptation without design.
1905 (photoelectric effect, special relativity; the "miracle year" also covered Brownian motion and atoms) and 1915 (general relativity): rewrote space, time, and gravity.

modules.summary: Propositional logic, truth tables, quantifiers, and the four proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction) — the reasoning substrate for policies, algorithms, and security arguments. Prerequisite spine for Humanities.
objectives: Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables and identify tautologies.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Humanities
Propositions, connectives, and truth tables
Tautologies, contradictions, and De Morgan’s laws
notes.body: A tautology is true in every row (e.g., p∨¬p); a contradiction is false in every row (p∧¬p). Two formulas are logically equivalent if their tables match column-for-column. Worked example (verified): prove De Morgan’s law ¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q by table. Row (T,T): LHS ¬T=F; RHS F∨F=F. Row (T,F): LHS ¬F=T; RHS F∨T=T. Row (F,T): LHS T; RHS T∨F=T. Row (F,F): LHS T; RHS T∨T=T. All four rows agree — equivalence verified. The dual law ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q holds by the same check. These laws are the workhorses of simplifying firewall rules, IAM policies, and boolean search: "not (A and B)" becomes "not-A or not-B". Other key equivalences: contrapositive (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p), and implication-as-disjunction (p→q ≡ ¬p∨q).

notes.title: Predicates and quantifiers
notes.body: A predicate P(x) becomes a proposition when x is fixed. Quantifiers bind x: ∀x P(x) ("for all x") and ∃x P(x) ("there exists x"). Worked example: let domain be integers, P(x) = "x² ≥ 0". Then ∀x P(x) is TRUE (squares are never negative). Now negate ∀x∃y (y > x) — "for every integer there is a larger one". Negation flips each quantifier and the inner predicate: ∃x∀y (y ≤ x) — "some integer is ≥ every integer", which is FALSE over integers (no maximum). The duality rules: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Common error: negating "all users are admins" as "no users are admins" — the correct negation is "some user is not an admin". In access-control requirements, this distinction is the difference between a correct policy and a breach.

notes.title: Direct proof and proof by contrapositive
notes.body: A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion through valid steps. Proof by contrapositive proves ¬q→¬p instead of p→q (equivalent by the table). Worked example: prove "if n² is even, then n is even" for integers. Direct attack stalls (square roots of parity are awkward), so use contrapositive: "if n is odd, then n² is odd". Let n = 2k+1. Then n² = 4k²+4k+1 = 2(2k²+2k)+1, which is odd. Contrapositive proved, so the original holds. Numeric check: n=7 (odd) → 49 (odd) ✓; n=6 (even) → 36 (even) ✓. Choose the method by shape: when the conclusion is a negative or "not" statement, contrapositive usually simplifies; when hypothesis and conclusion are both positive constructions, go direct.

notes.title: Proof by contradiction
notes.body: Assume the negation of what you want, derive an impossibility, and conclude the original. Worked example (classic, verified): prove √2 is irrational. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a,b)=1). Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, hence a is even (by the previous note’s result), a = 2k. Then 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² — b² is even, hence b is even. But a and b both even contradicts lowest terms. The assumption is impossible; √2 is irrational. The pattern: contradiction proofs shine when the claim says something does NOT exist (no rational square root, no largest prime). Euclid’s proof of infinitely many primes uses the same skeleton: assume finitely many, multiply them and add 1, find a new prime factor — contradiction.

notes.title: Mathematical induction

cards.back: A statement that is unambiguously true or false — never both, never neither.
Only when p is true and q is false. All other rows are true (vacuous truth).
¬(p∧q) ≡ ¬p∨¬q and ¬(p∨q) ≡ ¬p∧¬q — verified by truth table.
∃x ¬P(x). Quantifier flips; inner predicate negates.

cards.front: What is the contrapositive of p→q?
cards.back: ¬q→¬p — logically equivalent to the original.

cards.front: What is a tautology? A contradiction?
cards.back: Tautology: true in every truth-table row (p∨¬p). Contradiction: false in every row (p∧¬p).
Assume the negation of the claim; derive an impossibility; conclude the claim holds.

cards.front: The two steps of mathematical induction?
cards.back: Base case P(n₀); inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.front: Prove: if n² is even then n is even. Method?
cards.back: Contrapositive: n odd ⇒ n=2k+1 ⇒ n²=2(2k²+2k)+1, odd.

quiz.q: p=F, q=T. What is p→q?

handsOnLab.title: Verify logic by brute force with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify De Morgan’s laws and the contrapositive equivalence by exhaustive truth-table enumeration in Python, then prove a small parity claim both by hand and by exhaustive check. The machine settles every row; your hand proof must agree.
steps: Open python3. Define implies = lambda p,q: (not p) or q.
Enumerate all four (p,q) pairs. For each, compute not (p and q) and (not p) or (not q); assert they are equal on every row — De Morgan verified by brute force.
Repeat for the dual law: not (p or q) vs (not p) and (not q). Assert equality on all rows.
Verify contrapositive: for all rows, implies(p,q) == implies(not q, not p). Print any counterexample (there will be none).
Show the converse is NOT equivalent: find the row where implies(p,q) != implies(q,p). Record it.
Prove by hand on paper: "if n² is odd then n is odd" via contrapositive. Then brute-force check n in range(0,50): assert (n*n % 2 == 1) implies (n % 2 == 1).
Write up: which equivalences held on all rows, the converse counterexample row, and your parity proof.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A short write-up with the brute-force verification output, the converse counterexample, and the hand parity proof.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All assertions pass; the converse counterexample row is identified; the hand proof matches the brute-force check.

modules.title: Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Humanities
modules.summary: Descriptive statistics, probability rules, Bayes’ theorem, expectation and variance, the binomial and normal distributions, and hypothesis testing — the math behind evaluation metrics, alert triage, and A/B decisions. Prerequisite spine for Humanities.
objectives: Compute mean, median, variance, and standard deviation of a dataset.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules of probability.
Use Bayes’ theorem to update beliefs with evidence.
Compute expectation and variance of discrete random variables.

notes.title: Why this math matters for Humanities
Describing data: center and spread
Probability rules that never change
notes.body: Sample space S, event A: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, P(S) = 1. Addition rule: P(A∪b) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B) (subtract the double-counted overlap); for mutually exclusive events the last term is 0. Complement: P(not A) = 1−P(A). Multiplication: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(B|A)=P(B). Worked example (verified): a queue has 30% high-priority tickets (H) and 20% are escalations (E); 12% are both. P(H∪E) = 0.30+0.20−0.12 = 0.38. If instead H and E were independent, P(both) would be 0.30×0.20 = 0.06 ≠ 0.12 — so they are NOT independent (escalations skew high-priority). Two independent deploys each fail with p=0.05: P(both fail) = 0.05² = 0.0025; P(at least one fails) = 1−(0.95)² = 1−0.9025 = 0.0975.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem
notes.body: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B): probability of A given B occurred. Bayes inverts the conditioning: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+). Worked example — alert triage (verified): 1% of hosts are compromised (P(D)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of compromised hosts (sensitivity P(+|D)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of clean hosts (P(+|¬D)=0.05). P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099+0.0495 = 0.0594. P(D|+) = 0.0099/0.0594 ≈ 0.1667 — only ~16.7%! Most alerts are false positives despite a "99% accurate" detector, because the base rate is tiny. This base-rate effect is the single most important probability lesson for SOC triage, medical screening, and fraud detection: accuracy without the base rate is meaningless. Always expand P(+) via total probability before trusting a positive.

notes.title: Expectation and variance of random variables
notes.body: For discrete X with values xᵢ and probabilities pᵢ: E[X] = Σxᵢpᵢ (long-run average); Var(X) = E[X²]−(E[X])²; SD = √Var. Linearity: E[aX+b] = aE[X]+b, and E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when dependent. Worked example — fair die (verified): E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. E[X²] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.1667. Var = 91/6 − 3.5² = 15.1667−12.25 = 2.9167 = 35/12. SD ≈ 1.708. Worked example 2: a Bernoulli trial with success p has E[X]=p and Var=p(1−p) — variance peaks at p=0.5 (maximum uncertainty). In ML, cross-entropy loss is minimized exactly when predicted probabilities match these expectations; in capacity planning, E[load] sizes the average but Var(load) sizes the headroom.

notes.title: The binomial and normal distributions
notes.body: Binomial(n,p): number of successes in n independent trials; P(X=k) = C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k), E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p). Normal(μ,σ²): the bell curve; the 68-95-99.7 rule says P(|X−μ|<σ)≈0.68, <2σ ≈0.95, <3σ ≈0.997. Worked example — binomial (verified): 5 independent alert rules, each fires spuriously with p=0.3. P(exactly 2 fire) = C(5,2)·0.3²·0.7³ = 10×0.09×0.343 = 0.3087 ≈ 30.9%. Worked example — normal: API latency ~ Normal(μ=120ms, σ=15ms). P(latency > 150) = P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.0228 — about 2.3% of requests. The Central Limit Theorem is why the normal appears everywhere: averages of many small independent effects are approximately normal, which justifies z-intervals for A/B test readouts and poll margins.

notes.title: Hypothesis testing and confidence, honestly

cards.back: Mean = Σx/n (pulled by outliers: [12,15,13,90,14] → 28.8); median = middle value (14) — robust.
s² = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²/(n−1); standard deviation s = √s².
P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Subtract the overlap; mutually exclusive ⇒ last term 0.
P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(B|A) = P(B).
P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D)/P(+), with P(+) expanded by total probability.
With 1% prevalence and 5% false-alarm rate, P(compromised|alert) ≈ 16.7% — most alerts are false.

cards.front: E[X] and Var(X) for a fair die?

cards.back: C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k); E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p).
For Normal(μ,σ): ≈68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ of μ.
P(data this extreme | H₀) — not P(H₀ true). Reject H₀ when p < α.

cards.front: Why report effect size with p-values?
cards.back: "Significant" ≠ important; with 20 metrics tested, one hits p<0.05 by chance.

handsOnLab.title: Verify probability by simulation with Python
handsOnLab.brief: You will verify the Bayes triage calculation, the binomial probability, and the die variance three ways: by hand formula, by exact computation, and by Monte Carlo simulation. All three must agree.
steps: Open python3. Simulate the Bayes scenario: 1M hosts, 1% compromised; detector: 99% sensitivity, 5% false-alarm. Count positives and the fraction compromised among them; confirm ≈0.167.
Compute exactly: (0.99*0.01)/(0.99*0.01+0.05*0.99). Compare with the simulation to 3 decimals.
Binomial check: from math import comb; compute comb(5,2)*0.3**2*0.7**3; then simulate 200k runs of 5 Bernoulli(0.3) trials and compare the fraction with exactly 2 successes.
Die variance: exact = sum(x*x for x in range(1,7))/6 - 3.5**2; simulate 500k die rolls, compute sample variance; compare.
Break it: change prevalence to 50% in the Bayes simulation and watch P(D|+) jump — record both values to feel the base-rate effect.
Write up: the three agreements (formula vs exact vs simulation) and one sentence on why simulation is a legitimate verification tool.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Write-up with the three verified numbers (Bayes ≈0.1667, binomial ≈0.3087, die variance ≈2.9167) from all three methods.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Simulation, exact computation, and hand formula agree to 2+ decimals on all three quantities.

scriptLabs.title: Argument mapping: dissect a live proposal
scriptLabs.brief: Take a real technical proposal — an RFC, a vendor pitch, or a design doc — and map its argument structure: claims, premises, warrants, backing, and rebuttals. Uses the Toulmin model from the Rhetoric module.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Argument map: <proposal title>
# 1. MAIN CLAIM (the conclusion being argued for):
# 2. PREMISES (numbered — what the claim rests on):
# 3. WARRANT (the inference rule connecting premises to claim):
# 4. BACKING (evidence that the warrant is trustworthy):
# 5. REBUTTAL (the strongest counter-argument, steel-manned):
# 6. VERDICT (valid? sound? what evidence would change your mind?):
scriptLabs.hint: The warrant is the step most proposals skip: WHY do these premises imply this claim? State it explicitly, then ask whether the backing actually supports it.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Argument map: Adopt Postgres for the billing service
# 1. MAIN CLAIM: Migrate billing from MySQL to Postgres in Q1.
# 2. PREMISES: (a) Billing needs serializable transactions across shards. (b) Our MySQL setup cannot do cross-shard serializable writes. (c) Postgres 16 handles our peak write load in benchmarks.
# 3. WARRANT: If the current store cannot meet a hard requirement and the candidate can, migration is justified.
# 4. BACKING: Benchmark report 2026-09 (appendix A); two incident postmortems citing the MySQL limitation.
# 5. REBUTTAL (steel-manned): Migration risk exceeds the benefit — the serializable requirement occurs in 0.1% of transactions, and application-level sagas would cover it without a database migration.
# 6. VERDICT: Valid form; soundness hinges on premise (a) — if the 0.1% figure is right, the warrant's 'hard requirement' framing fails. Request the transaction-mix data before deciding.

scriptLabs.title: Close reading: charity pass on a hard text
scriptLabs.brief: Perform a two-pass close reading of a short philosophical excerpt (the module suggests Mill on liberty or a passage from the course notes): first a charity pass reconstructing the strongest version of the argument, then a critical pass testing its premises.
scriptLabs.starter:
# Close reading: <text and passage>
# CHARITY PASS (strongest reconstruction):
# - The author's central claim, in your own words:
# - The premises, numbered, as the author would defend them:
# CRITICAL PASS:
# - PREMISES under pressure (which is weakest, and why):
# - OBJECTION (the best one-sentence objection):
# - CHARITABLE REPLY (how the author might answer it):
# VERDICT: what survives the critical pass?
scriptLabs.hint: Do the charity pass fully before any criticism — write the version of the argument the author's smartest defender would endorse. Only then attack. Reversing the order produces straw men.
scriptLabs.solution:
# Close reading: Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1 (harm principle passage)
# CHARITY PASS: The state (or society) may coerce an individual only to prevent harm to others; the individual's own good is never sufficient warrant. Premises: (1) human fallibility makes any censor likely wrong sometimes; (2) truth emerges from open contest; (3) individuality is a constitutive part of well-being, not a luxury.
# CRITICAL PASS: Premise (3) is the load-bearing one — a critic who denies that individuality matters can accept (1) and (2) and still regulate. OBJECTION: the harm principle under-determines cases like hate speech, where 'harm' itself is contested. CHARITABLE REPLY: Mill would distinguish offense from harm and demand the critic show concrete injury.
# VERDICT: the epistemic argument (fallibility + contest) survives even if you reject the individuality premise — it independently supports free expression.

scenarios.title: AI Deployment Ethics Review
scenarios.context: Your team built a resume-screening model. It is 12% more 'accurate' than human screeners on historical data, but an audit shows it downgrades resumes with employment gaps — disproportionately affecting caregivers returning to work. Leadership wants to ship Friday.

steps.prompt: How do you frame the decision?

options.text: Run the three-traditions analysis before deciding: duties, consequences, and character
options.why: The traditions structure the trade-off instead of letting urgency decide: deontology flags treating applicants as mere means, consequentialism weighs aggregate hiring gains vs. harms, virtue asks what a good craftsperson ships.

options.text: Ship it — 12% accuracy gain is the only metric that matters
options.why: Accuracy on biased historical data is not the same as a good hiring decision; the metric begs the question.

options.text: Kill the project quietly without analysis
options.why: Avoidance without reasoning teaches the org nothing and may forfeit real benefits a constrained deployment could capture.

steps.prompt: Analysis done. What do you recommend?

options.text: Constrained pilot: remove the gap-penalizing features, add human review of edge cases, instrument outcomes, revisit in 90 days
options.why: Collingridge-aware: reversible, monitored, humble. It captures value while containing the foreseeable harm — and generates the data a fuller decision needs.

options.text: Full deployment with a fairness statement on the website
options.why: A statement doesn't change the model's behavior; this is ethics theater.

options.text: Hand the decision to legal alone
options.why: Legal sets the floor, not the ceiling — 'lawful' and 'right' are different questions.

scenarios.title: The Dual-Use Dilemma
scenarios.context: Your open-source computer-vision library — built for wildlife conservation — is being forked for automated targeting in a conflict zone. Contributors are split: pull the repo, or keep shipping?

steps.prompt: First, how do you think about it?

options.text: Dual-use analysis: same mechanism, divergent uses — ask which uses, under what controls
options.why: Neither 'technology is neutral' nor 'ban everything' survives contact with the case; the serious question is always about specific uses and controls.

options.text: It's neutral — tools have no moral character
options.why: Affordances shape use; a targeting-ready vision stack is not morally identical to a spreadsheet.
Deletion also kills the conservation work and won't un-publish the forks — consequences matter too.

steps.prompt: What concrete step best fits the analysis?

options.text: Keep the conservation core open; gate the targeting-enabling modules behind review, document foreseeable misuse, add a use policy
options.why: Differentiated controls: preserve the benign use, add friction to the harmful one, document the reasoning — the engineer's four moves.

options.text: Do nothing — open source means no control
options.why: License terms, module structure, and documentation are all levers; 'no control' is false.
Deception violates professional duties and destroys the trust the conservation work depends on.

scenarios.title: Writing Under Pressure
scenarios.context: A Sev-1 outage just ended. You must write the incident review: it will be read by engineers, executives, and possibly a customer. The root cause implicates a shortcut your own team took.

options.text: BLUF: impact and resolution first, then timeline, root cause (honest), action items with owners
options.why: Scanners get the essentials in paragraph one; the honest root cause preserves credibility; owned actions make it a tool, not a ritual.

options.text: Chronological narrative from the first alert
options.why: Chronology buries the conclusion; busy readers never reach the decisions.

options.text: Emphasize external factors to protect the team
options.why: Selective framing is manipulation; blameless review requires honest causation — blame the system, describe it truthfully.

steps.prompt: How do you phrase the team's shortcut?

options.text: State it plainly with the reasoning at the time, then the systemic fix that removes the temptation
options.why: Honest, blameless, and forward-looking: it names the cause without personal attack and fixes the incentive.

options.text: Omit it — the fix is what matters
options.why: Omitting known causation corrupts the record and guarantees recurrence.

options.text: Name and shame the engineer who took it
options.why: Blame ends learning; the next shortcut will just be hidden better.

mockTasks.q: Which branch asks 'What can we know?'
mockTasks.explain: Epistemology is the theory of knowledge — its nature, sources, and limits.

mockTasks.q: The principle of charity requires:
mockTasks.explain: Charity means engaging the strongest form of the argument, not a weak caricature.

mockTasks.q: Philosophy of mind is most relevant to which technical debate?
mockTasks.explain: Questions about what minds are — and whether machines could have them — are philosophy of mind.

mockTasks.q: An argument consists of:
mockTasks.explain: The logical structure: premises support the conclusion via an inference.

mockTasks.q: 'All servers are machines; db-1 is a server; therefore db-1 is a machine' is:
mockTasks.explain: Correct form (syllogism) with true premises — valid and sound.

mockTasks.q: 'Either we migrate now or the system collapses' — with no evidence of collapse — is:
mockTasks.explain: It asserts only two options without ruling out the rest — the false-dilemma pattern.

mockTasks.q: Inferring 'the cache is stale' as the best explanation of the symptoms is:
mockTasks.explain: Best-explanation inference from evidence — abduction, the logic of debugging.

mockTasks.q: 'The CTO prefers Postgres, so Postgres is the right choice' is:
mockTasks.explain: Status substitutes for reasons — the CTO's preference is not itself an argument.

mockTasks.q: 'Would I endorse everyone doing this?' is the decision procedure of:
mockTasks.explain: Universalizability is Kant's test — the first formulation of the categorical imperative.

mockTasks.q: A utilitarian evaluates shipping a risky feature by:
mockTasks.explain: Consequentialism judges by outcomes — expected benefits weighed against expected harms.

mockTasks.q: Aristotle's term for flourishing through virtuous activity?
mockTasks.explain: Eudaimonia — often translated flourishing — is the telos of the virtuous life. (Arete is virtue/excellence itself.)

mockTasks.q: Treating users 'merely as means' would be condemned by:
mockTasks.explain: The humanity formulation: never treat rational agents merely as instruments.

mockTasks.q: The Collingridge dilemma implies designers should favor:
mockTasks.explain: Since early knowledge is poor and late change is hard, keep options open and design for reversibility.

mockTasks.q: Facial recognition is best described as:
mockTasks.explain: Same mechanism serves security/authentication and mass surveillance — the question is which uses under what controls.

mockTasks.q: 'The model did it' as a defense fails because:
choices: Professionals retain responsibility for foreseeable system behavior
mockTasks.explain: Professional responsibility covers foreseeable misuse of systems you design and deploy.

mockTasks.q: The ACM Code of Ethics (2018) is best used as:
choices: A decision oracle for hard cases
A floor and shared language for escalation
mockTasks.explain: Codes set minimums and give practitioners vocabulary to raise concerns — they don't automate judgment.

mockTasks.q: A theory compatible with every possible observation is, for Popper:
mockTasks.explain: Falsifiability is the demarcation line: no forbidden observations, no science.

mockTasks.q: Gettier cases show that:
choices: Justified true belief can be accidentally true
mockTasks.explain: Gettier constructed JTB cases where the belief is true by luck — intuitively not knowledge.

mockTasks.q: In Kuhn's account, a paradigm determines:
choices: What counts as a legitimate problem and solution
mockTasks.explain: Paradigms structure normal science — its questions, methods, and standards of success.

mockTasks.q: Pre-registration primarily combats:
mockTasks.explain: Locking in hypotheses and analyses before seeing data removes the garden of forking paths.

mockTasks.q: Ptolemy's Almagest is best described as:
choices: A geocentric model, predictively strong for 1400 years
mockTasks.explain: Epicycles were structurally wrong but predicted planetary positions well — a lesson in prediction vs. truth.

mockTasks.q: The word 'algorithm' derives from:
mockTasks.explain: The 9th-century scholar's name, Latinized, attached to his systematic procedures.

mockTasks.q: Galileo's 1633 condemnation concerned:
mockTasks.explain: The Inquisition's trial centered on his defense of the Copernican system.

mockTasks.q: Kepler derived his laws primarily from:
mockTasks.explain: Brahe's unprecedentedly precise naked-eye data made the ellipses detectable.

mockTasks.q: Maxwell's equations unified:
mockTasks.explain: One framework for electric and magnetic fields, with light as an electromagnetic wave.

mockTasks.q: Hertz's 1887 experiments confirmed:
mockTasks.explain: Hertz generated and detected radio waves — the waves Maxwell's theory required.

mockTasks.q: Turing's 1936 paper established:
choices: The theoretical model of universal computation
mockTasks.explain: The universal Turing machine defined computability before electronic computers existed.

mockTasks.q: The transistor (1947) rested on which science?
mockTasks.explain: Band theory and semiconductor physics are quantum-mechanical — 1920s theory, 1940s device.

mockTasks.q: The Second Industrial Revolution is associated with:
mockTasks.explain: ~1870–1914: electrification, Bessemer steel, chemical industry, internal combustion.

mockTasks.q: Moore's 'chasm' lies between:
choices: Early adopters and the early majority
mockTasks.explain: Crossing from enthusiasts to the pragmatic majority is the go-to-market crux.

mockTasks.q: A disruptive technology, in Christensen's sense, typically starts:
choices: Worse and cheaper, serving overlooked customers
mockTasks.explain: Disruption enters low-end or new markets, then moves up as performance improves.

mockTasks.q: TCP/IP standardization (1983) mattered because:
choices: It created a common open layer enabling the internet's growth
mockTasks.explain: An open, shared protocol layer let diverse networks interoperate — infrastructure for everything above.

mockTasks.q: Which sentence is strongest?
choices: The service is restarted by the script.
The deploy script restarts the service.
It is important to note the service gets restarted.
mockTasks.explain: Concrete subject, active verb, no throat-clearing.

mockTasks.q: BLUF means:
mockTasks.explain: Lead with the conclusion so scanners can triage.

mockTasks.q: A runbook is tested by:
choices: Someone who didn't write it, during calm
mockTasks.explain: Only a fresh reader proves the runbook is self-sufficient; never first-test it in a real incident.

mockTasks.q: 'Latency got much worse' should become:
mockTasks.explain: Numbers beat adjectives — precise, checkable, actionable.

mockTasks.q: Citing your team's incident-free record to support a proposal appeals to:
mockTasks.explain: Credibility of the speaker — ethos. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: In Toulmin's model, the warrant is:
choices: The inference license from grounds to claim
mockTasks.explain: The warrant is why the grounds support the claim — usually the contested part. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Presenting only the metrics that favor your proposal is:
mockTasks.explain: Bypassing rational agency with selective evidence — manipulation, not persuasion. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Framing the same migration as 'risk reduction' to ops and 'feature velocity' to product is an example of:
mockTasks.explain: Framing selects which aspects are salient for an audience — honest when it foregrounds relevant aspects. (Module 10: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: A price ceiling set below equilibrium causes:
mockTasks.explain: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: $2M already spent on a failing project. The next phase costs $200K for $150K of value. Rational choice?
choices: Stop — the $2M is sunk; marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit
mockTasks.explain: Sunk costs are irrelevant; at the margin, $200K > $150K, so stop. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Software has high fixed and near-zero marginal cost, so it exhibits:
mockTasks.explain: Average cost collapses as users grow — the economics of the whole industry. (Module 11: Concepts.)

choices: Supply shifts right; price falls, quantity rises
mockTasks.explain: Lower input cost shifts supply right — the standard supply-shock result. (Module 11: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: A factory's smoke harms neighbors. This is a:
mockTasks.explain: A cost imposed on third parties outside the transaction. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, the Nash equilibrium is:
mockTasks.explain: Each player gains by defecting regardless of the other's move — defection dominates. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Tit-for-tat sustains cooperation in repeated games because:
choices: Retaliation makes defection unprofitable over time
mockTasks.explain: The shadow of future retaliation shifts the equilibrium toward cooperation. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Congestion pricing on a highway is an example of:
mockTasks.explain: It charges drivers the congestion cost they impose — designing the payoff matrix. (Module 12: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: An open-source license (e.g., MIT) is legally:
mockTasks.explain: Copyright vests automatically; the license is the author's permission slip with conditions. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: GDPR's data minimization principle requires:
choices: Collecting only data needed for the stated purpose
Storing data only in the EU
mockTasks.explain: Purpose limitation + minimization: collect what the purpose needs, nothing more. (Module 13: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: Technical standards (IETF, NIST) become binding when:
choices: Referenced by law, contract, or procurement
mockTasks.explain: Standards are voluntary until legislation, regulation, or contracts incorporate them. (Module 13: Concepts.)

choices: The integration of multiple lenses on ends as well as means
mockTasks.explain: Judgment = structured thinking about what is worth doing, using every lens. (Module 14: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: When asked 'is this system fair?', the skilled response:
choices: Answer it as a values question with reasons
mockTasks.explain: Values questions deserve values reasoning — metrics alone dodge the question. (Module 14: Concepts.)

mockTasks.q: The through-line connecting all six humanities areas is:
choices: Structured reasoning about human ends and means
mockTasks.explain: Each area is a discipline of thinking about what matters and why — in service of better building. (Module 14: Concepts.)

blocks.body:
- Modus ponens: P→Q, P ⊢ Q
- Modus tollens: P→Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P
- Valid = form; sound = valid + true premises

- Ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, post hoc
- Appeal to authority, begging the question, slippery slope
- Name it, then give the substantive reply

- Claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal
- Fights are usually about warrants

- Virtue (Aristotle): what kind of person? Habits, character.
- Deontology (Kant): duty; universalizable maxims; persons as ends.
- Consequentialism (Bentham/Mill): maximize good outcomes.

- Collingridge: design reversible, anticipatory, humble
- Dual use: which uses, under what controls?
- Document misuse, add friction, instrument, preserve override

- BLUF; headings; short paragraphs
- Active voice, concrete subjects, numbers over adjectives
- Define terms; cut 20% on second pass

- Ethos, pathos, logos (Aristotle)
- Audience: values, knowledge, decision criteria
- Persuasion respects agency; manipulation bypasses it

- ~700 BCE: Babylonian astronomy, base-60 arithmetic
- ~300 BCE: Euclid's Elements — the axiomatic method
- 3rd c. BCE: Archimedes — buoyancy, levers, pi by polygons
- 2nd c. CE: Ptolemy's Almagest — epicycles (wrong, predictive)
- 8th–13th c.: Al-Khwarizmi (algebra → 'algorithm'), Ibn al-Haytham (optics)
- 1543: Copernicus — heliocentrism
- 1609–1619: Kepler's laws from Brahe's data
- 1609 / 1633: Galileo — telescope; house arrest
- 1687: Newton's Principia — motion + universal gravitation

- 1859: Darwin — natural selection
- 1860s: Maxwell unifies electricity, magnetism, light; Hertz confirms (1887)
- 1900: Planck quantizes energy
- 1905 / 1915: Einstein — special, then general relativity
- 1920s: quantum mechanics (Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac)
- 1936: Turing — the universal machine
- 1948: Shannon — information theory
- 1945–1969: ENIAC, transistor, integrated circuits, ARPANET

- S-curve: slow uptake → explosive growth → saturation
- Chasm (Moore): early adopters → early majority
- Innovator's Dilemma (Christensen, 1997): disruption from below
- Kodak (1975, Sasson) invented the digital camera and lost
- Internet: ARPANET (1969) → TCP/IP (1983) → Web (1990–); open protocols won

- Opportunity cost: the best forgone alternative
- Marginal analysis: decide on the next unit
- Fixed vs variable vs sunk (sunk is ignored)
- TCO: license + integration + ops + opportunity cost + maintenance
- Price ceiling below equilibrium → shortage; floor above → surplus

- Nash equilibrium: no unilateral deviation pays
- Prisoner's dilemma: mutual defection stable, mutual cooperation better
- Escapes: repetition (tit-for-tat), contracts, reputation, new payoffs
- Mechanism design: set rules so self-interest yields the desired outcome
- Externality: third-party cost/benefit; price it, assign rights (Coase), or fund it

- Copyright: expression, automatic (MIT/GPL are copyright licenses)
- Patent: inventions, ~20yr; Trademark: brand marks; Trade secret: secrecy
- GDPR (EU, 2018): consent, minimization, purpose limitation, erasure
- CCPA/CPRA: opt-out of sale/sharing, deletion; HIPAA: health; COPPA: children
- Standards bind when referenced by law, contract, or procurement
- Literacy, not legal advice
An argument is valid if the conclusion *must* be true when premises are true. Sound = valid + true premises. Validity is about form, not truth.
Deduction: guaranteed (modus ponens). Induction: probable generalization from cases. Abduction: inference to the best explanation (diagnosis, debugging).

Ad hominem (attack the person) · strawman (attack a caricature) · false dilemma (two options only) · slippery slope (no mechanism) · appeal to authority (wrong domain) · begging the question (conclusion in premises) · survivorship (ignore the failures).
Name the fallacy *and* show the repaired argument. 'That's a strawman' without the steelman is just heckling.

cheatSheets.title: Ethics — three traditions for technology dilemmas

blocks.body: What would the flourishing practitioner do? (Aristotle) Focus: character, habits, practical wisdom. Ask: does this make us the kind of builders we want to be?
Duties and rules that bind regardless of outcome (Kant). Ask: could this be a universal rule? Are we treating users as ends, not means?
Maximize good outcomes (Bentham/Mill). Ask: expected benefits minus harms, across all affected, over time.
Run the dilemma through all three. When they agree, decide. When they conflict, the conflict *is* the analysis — document it.

cheatSheets.title: Writing & rhetoric — BLUF, active voice, Toulmin

blocks.body: Bottom Line Up Front: conclusion first, then supporting detail. Busy readers decide in the first sentence.
'The server rejected the request' beats 'the request was rejected by the server.' Actor → action → object.
Claim → grounds (evidence) → warrant (why grounds support claim) → qualifier → rebuttal (limits). Every paragraph earns its claim.
Logos (reason), pathos (emotion), ethos (credibility). Technical writing leads with logos but never ignores ethos.
The value of the best forgone alternative. Every 'yes' is a 'no' to something else — price it.
People respond to incentives (Goodhart's law for metrics). Externalities: costs/benefits falling on third parties — the market-failure pattern behind regulation.
Nash equilibrium: no unilateral deviation pays. Prisoner's dilemma: individually rational → collectively bad. Mechanism design: build the game so good play wins.
Statute → regulation → case law: the hierarchy. Read for obligations, definitions, and penalties. You're a literate citizen, not counsel — know when to call counsel.

cheatSheets.title: Philosophy of science & history of tech

blocks.body: Scientific claims stick their necks out: they say what would prove them wrong. Unfalsifiable = not science (yet).
Normal science puzzles within a paradigm; anomalies accumulate → crisis → revolution. Expect resistance to the new frame.
One study is a rumor. Pre-registration, replication, meta-analysis: the credibility stack. Apply to every 'study shows' headline.
Antiquity (geometry, logic) → Islamic golden age (algebra, optics) → Scientific Revolution → Industrial → information age. Each era's tools shape its questions.

answerBank.q: Argue for or against deploying a hiring model that is more accurate on average but disadvantages one group.
answerBank.a: Framework: (1) Epistemology — what does 'accurate' mean on biased labels? (2) Deontology — does it treat applicants as ends? (3) Consequentialism — aggregate gains vs. concentrated harms, including second-order effects on the applicant pool. (4) Reversibility — can the decision be undone and monitored? A defensible answer works all four and lands on a constrained, monitored pilot or a no-go with reasons — never on the metric alone.

answerBank.q: Is open-sourcing a powerful model dual-use? What follows?
answerBank.a: Framework: identify the mechanism's affordances for benign and harmful uses separately; assess how much the release *marginally* enables harm versus the status quo; consider controls (staged release, use policies, monitoring). 'Neutral' and 'ban it' are both evasions — the answer is always which uses under what controls, with the reasoning documented.

answerBank.q: Explain a technical trade-off to a non-technical executive.
answerBank.a: Framework: stakes first (what changes for them), options with honest trade-offs, recommendation with reasons. One defined term per jargon item, or none. End with the decision you need from them and by when. Anticipate the values question ('is it fair/safe?') and answer it as a values question.

answerBank.q: A paper claims a breakthrough. How do you read it as an epistemologist?
answerBank.a: Framework: Popper — what would falsify it? Kuhn — which paradigm does it extend or challenge? Replication — sample size, pre-registration, effect size with uncertainty, independent replication. Treat it as conjecture until the field converges; never cite the press release.

answerBank.q: Build vs. buy: make the economic case.
answerBank.a: Framework: total cost of ownership over the realistic lifetime — license/fees + integration + operations + opportunity cost of diverted engineers + maintenance. Compare marginal costs at expected scale. Name the sunk-cost fallacy explicitly if past spend is invoked. Decide on forward-looking numbers.

answerBank.q: Your team is split on a rewrite. How do you decide?
answerBank.a: Framework: Toulmin — surface the warrants ('rewrites always fail' vs. 'the debt is fatal'), not just the data. Economics — opportunity cost of the rewrite vs. incremental repair. History — second-system effect (Brooks) as a caution. Decide with a time-boxed spike that could falsify the rewrite case.

terminalSims.title: Logic CLI drill
terminalSims.brief: Practice propositional-logic checks and argument-form identification against a canned shell. Type 'help' to list commands.

commands.out:
check <form>   test an argument form for validity
forms          list the named forms
quiz           a random argument to classify

Example: check "if P then Q; P; therefore Q"

modus ponens      if P then Q; P; therefore Q            (valid)
modus tollens     if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P    (valid)
affirm consequent if P then Q; Q; therefore P            (INVALID)
deny antecedent   if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q    (INVALID)
disj syllogism    P or Q; not P; therefore Q             (valid)

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; P; therefore Q"
commands.out: VALID — modus ponens. The conclusion follows necessarily.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P"
commands.out: VALID — modus tollens. Denying the consequent is the safe move.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; Q; therefore P"
commands.out: INVALID — affirming the consequent. Q may hold for other reasons.

commands.cmd: check "if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q"
commands.out: INVALID — denying the antecedent. P is sufficient, not necessary.

Classify: 'The cache is stale or the CDN is down. The cache is fresh. Therefore the CDN is down.'
(Type your answer, then: check "P or Q; not P; therefore Q" to verify.)

commands.cmd: check "P or Q; not P; therefore Q"
commands.out: VALID — disjunctive syllogism. Eliminating one disjunct leaves the other.

terminalSims.title: Argument workshop CLI
terminalSims.brief: Map claims and premises, test validity, and steel-man positions from the command line. Type 'help' to list commands.

commands.out:
map <claim>      scaffold a Toulmin map for a claim
steelman <view>   prompt the steel-man procedure
fallacy <name>   definition + example of a named fallacy

Example: fallacy strawman

CLAIM: we should migrate to Postgres
GROUNDS:    (list your evidence)
WARRANT:    (why do these grounds imply the claim?)
BACKING:    (why trust the warrant?)
REBUTTAL:   (strongest counter-case)
QUALIFIER:  (how confident — probably, certainly, plausibly?)

Strongest version: deploys stay atomic, cross-service transactions vanish, debugging is one process, and team cognitive load drops.
Now answer THAT — not the weak version ('monoliths are old').

Straw man: restating the opponent's position weakly to defeat it easily.
Antidote: steel-man first (see: steelman).

Post hoc ergo propter hoc: 'after it, therefore because of it.'
The deploy preceded the outage — correlation is not yet causation; check the evidence chain.

Not a fallacy — the principle of charity: reconstruct the strongest version of a claim before evaluating it.

faq.q: Why should a technologist study humanities?
faq.a: Because the hard problems are judgment problems: which system to build, whose values it encodes, how to argue for it honestly. Logic, ethics, economics, and rhetoric are the disciplines of judgment — the course's thesis.
None exclusively — the course teaches all three as lenses. Run dilemmas through each; agreement decides, disagreement *is* the analysis. Ethical maturity is holding the conflict, not picking a team.

faq.q: How do I evaluate a 'study shows' headline?
faq.a: Ask: pre-registered? replicated? effect size (not just p-value)? who funded it? One study is a rumor — the replication stack is the credibility test.
No — it's respect for the reader's time. Conclusion first, then the reasoning for those who want it. Rudeness is burying the answer on page three.

faq.q: Can I really read law without being a lawyer?
faq.a: As a literate citizen, yes: find the obligations, definitions, and penalties; track the hierarchy (statute → regulation → case). The course teaches when that suffices and when to call counsel.
Model the incentives, find the equilibria, then design the rules so the equilibrium you want is the one that's stable.

brief.text: You write the decision policy for an autonomous shuttle. A brake failure is unavoidable: swerve left into one pedestrian, or continue into five? The utilitarian, deontological, and virtue-ethics answers differ. Which tradition does your policy encode, and can you defend it publicly?

choices.label: Utilitarian: minimize harm — swerve
choices.feedback: A defensible position — but note what it commits you to: the policy now trades lives by arithmetic. The module's point is not the answer; it is that shipping the system IS choosing a tradition, whether you name it or not.

choices.label: Deontological: never use a person as a mere means — do not swerve
choices.feedback: A defensible position — but note the cost: five deaths you could have prevented by acting. Deontology forbids using the one, even to save five. Name the tradition in the design doc, or the choice gets made by accident.

choices.label: Refuse to encode any — kick it to a human
choices.feedback: There is no human to kick it to at 60 mph — the refusal IS a policy (continue straight). Every deployed system encodes an ethic. The only choice is whether it is examined.

branchingScenarios.title: Argue the budget: make the case

ask.text: Leadership will fund either the security overhaul or the feature team — not both. You have ten minutes. Do you open with data, story, or authority?

choices.label: Story: the 2 AM outage, then the numbers
choices.feedback: Strong open — narrative buys attention, then numbers buy the decision. But watch the failure mode: if the story doesn't connect to the ask within 90 seconds, you've told an anecdote, not made a case.

choices.label: Data: lead with the incident-cost table
choices.feedback: Respectable — and the fastest way to lose a non-technical room. Data persuades after attention is won; lead with it only if the room already trusts the premise.

choices.label: Authority: quote the CISO's own memo
choices.feedback: Effective if the authority is present and aligned; borrowed authority collapses under one skeptical question. Prefer evidence you can defend yourself.
